clue.text: Ahab's Pequod is internally sound

parts.note: Captain Ahab's ship in Moby-Dick hunts leviathans, and the word for such a vessel holds HALE, meaning sound or healthy, in its middle letters

explanation.surface: A remark on the seaworthiness of Captain Ahab's ship in Moby-Dick.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pequod is the vessel of Melville's novel; the cryptic twist is that the word for it carries HALE (sound, healthy) inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pequod was a nineteenth-century Nantucket ship hunting sperm whales for oil.

clue.text: Jump on board for a game

definitions.text: Jump on board for a game

parts.words: Jump on board for a game
parts.note: a Victorian board game in which pieces hop over others, its name being Greek for leap

explanation.surface: Someone hops aboard to join in some play.
explanation.walkthrough: The game's name is the Greek for 'jump', and its pieces jump across a chequered board.
explanation.definitionFit: A board game invented in the 1880s, named from the Greek for leap.

clue.text: No truth about change of scene for innkeepers

indicators.note: about means the first piece is wrapped round the second

parts.note: lies are untruths

indicators.note: change of means the letters of the next word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that pub landlords lie about a change of setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No truth' reads as a denial but is a noun phrase for untruths; 'change of' asks for the following word to be rearranged, and 'about' wraps the untruths round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Publicans hold licences to sell alcohol, so they are licence holders.

clue.text: Revolt Is where the Boxers are

definitions.meaning: the Boxer Rebellion in China in 1900 is also called this uprising, and IS sits inside RING, where boxers fight

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition also hints at IS placed in RING, where boxers are found.
explanation.definitionFit: An uprising is a revolt, and the 1900 Chinese insurrection is named the Boxer one.

clue.text: Meekness causes one old city's ruin

indicators.note: a ruin is something wrecked, so the letters of the words before it are knocked down and rebuilt

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
the word city, with the possessive ending ignored

explanation.surface: A claim that a timid temperament brought down an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruin' tells you to rearrange I, OLD and CITY; the 's of city's is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Meekness and the answer are synonyms, both meaning a gentle readiness to be led.

clue.text: Not the predecessors of nude shows ?

definitions.text: Not the predecessors of nude shows ?

parts.words: Not the predecessors of nude shows ?
parts.note: a final run-through in full costume would hardly precede a performance with no clothes

explanation.surface: A remark on what comes before a striptease revue.
explanation.walkthrough: These final practices are done in costume, which a nude show would not need.
explanation.definitionFit: Final run-throughs of a stage show, done in full costume before opening night.

clue.text: Ability to go, one better than a Bristol team

parts.note: to cap something is to go one better than it
Bristol City is a football club

explanation.surface: A team's prowess compared with a Bristol football side.
explanation.walkthrough: Bristol City is a football club in the west of England; 'than' just joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Capacity can mean a power or ability to do something.

clue.text: Thrashes many Wimbledon winners

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, so many
aces are unreturned serves that win points at the Wimbledon tennis championships

explanation.surface: Plenty of tennis champions give their opponents a beating.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon is the London tennis tournament; L (50) is a common crossword 'many'.
explanation.definitionFit: To lace someone is old slang for beating or whipping them.

clue.text: Cruel sort of men in high places

indicators.note: in means the second piece sits within the first

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill on Dartmoor, so two high places give two tors
taken as written

explanation.surface: Men in positions of power are said to be brutal.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor in south-west England; MEN goes between two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who inflicts suffering on others is a cruel type.

clue.text: More than a pair of bags from this bad lot

definitions.text: More than a pair of bags from this
definitions.meaning: in the nursery rhyme the woolly animal gives three bags full, which is more than a pair
a disreputable member of a family or group

explanation.surface: A nursery-rhyme animal yields more wool than expected, but is a disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool? Yes sir, three bags full' supplies the first reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme's sheep gives three bags of wool, and the same phrase is idiom for the family's disgrace.

clue.text: Eccentric joker perhaps

definitions.meaning: an odd, amusing person is called this in British slang
the joker is one of the pack used in games

explanation.definitionFit: A comic oddball is colloquially a card, and the joker is one item in a deck of playing cards.

clue.text: 19 is one of these, of course

definitions.text: 19 is one of these, of course

parts.words: 19 is one of these, of course
parts.note: the answer to 19 across is the cry a golfer shouts on the course to alert players ahead

explanation.surface: A self-evident remark that a number belongs to some group.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 across is FORE, the golfer's shout; 'of course' looks like 'naturally' but means on the golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer's shout alerts people ahead that a ball is coming, so it is a cautionary signal.

clue.text: Furniture-mover's helper donning it for the races

definitions.meaning: a small swivelling wheel fixed under a chair or table leg so it can be pushed about
a castor or ... is also an old word for a hat, originally of beaver fur, worn to a race meeting

explanation.surface: A removal man's assistant puts on his best for a day at the races.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the old hat called a castor (from Latin for beaver); 'donning it' says the thing is something worn.
explanation.definitionFit: A swivel wheel helps shift heavy furniture, and a beaver hat was worn for smart outings like race meetings.

clue.text: But it sounds like the whole lot

definitions.text: But it sounds like the whole lot

parts.words: But it sounds like the whole lot
parts.note: the word means only a part or a few, yet when spoken it sounds like sum, the total

explanation.surface: A wry observation that a small quantity can pass for everything.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for a part of something is said exactly like SUM, the total: the 'But' sets up that contrast.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means an unspecified part or quantity, the opposite of a total.

clue.text: Method of working in the theatre

definitions.text: Method of working in the theatre

parts.words: Method of working in the theatre
parts.note: read the theatre as the hospital operating theatre, where surgeons perform procedures

explanation.surface: An actor's technique on the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'theatre' suggests a stage, but it is the surgeons' theatre; the word also means a way of working.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgical procedure takes place in an operating theatre, and the word also means a mode of functioning.

clue.text: Tiny tree, destroyed completely in this

indicators.note: destroyed means the two words before it are broken up and their letters rebuilt

explanation.surface: A small tree is wrecked from top to bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed' rearranges TINY and TREE; the definition works because 'completely' means 'in its whole extent', so the answer fills the 'this'.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something completely is doing it in its whole extent, so the answer names the complete whole.

clue.text: Where brothers take food in church house, with iron content.

indicators.note: content here means contained, so the first piece holds the second

parts.note: a rectory is the house of a parish priest
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: Monks eat in a parsonage that has iron fittings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' looks like satisfied but is stressed on the second syllable's sense of contained; brothers are monks, not siblings.
explanation.definitionFit: Monks and friars eat their meals in this communal dining hall of a monastery.

clue.text: Players ready for heaven?

parts.note: angels in heaven are traditionally pictured strumming a stringed instrument, so its musicians are already equipped

explanation.surface: Sportsmen who are ready for paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' suggests a team, but means musicians of the stringed instrument associated with angels.
explanation.definitionFit: Musicians who pluck the instrument that angels are pictured holding.

clue.text: One with whom one might get fed up ?

definitions.text: One with whom one might get fed up ?

parts.words: One with whom one might get fed up ?
parts.note: read 'fed up' not as bored but as served meals together in the same military dining hall

explanation.surface: Someone who eventually becomes tiresome company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fed up' looks like annoyed, but means literally fed alongside: a mess is where service people eat together.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess is a shared dining room on a ship or in barracks, and those eating there together are companions.

clue.text: But not the front of a Gilbert's ship

definitions.text: But not the front of a Gilbert's ship

parts.words: But not the front of a Gilbert's ship
parts.note: the bow of a ship is its forward part, but in Gilbert's HMS ... this word comes at the tail of the vessel's name

explanation.surface: A correction about which part of a vessel in a Gilbert opera is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: HMS Pinafore is the Gilbert and Sullivan opera; the answer means the front of a ship yet comes at the end of Pinafore.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the forward part of a ship, here the final letters of the opera's title.

clue.text: It's hot under these trees in Hampshire

definitions.text: It's hot under these trees in Hampshire

parts.words: It's hot under these trees in Hampshire
parts.note: the garrison town of ... in Hampshire is these trees with HOT placed after them

explanation.surface: A summer report on shade trees in a southern English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Hampshire is a county in southern England; its army town Aldershot splits as the trees plus HOT, which comes 'under' in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Trees of the birch family, common on damp ground.

clue.text: Frolicsome sort of headgear for a hatter?

definitions.meaning: an impulsive, reckless and lively person
the Mad Hatter of Alice in Wonderland might wear a cap to suit his name

explanation.definitionFit: A wild impetuous person is so called, and a crazed milliner's bonnet would be one literally.

clue.text: He should be able to compose a lyric

indicators.note: to compose is to put together, so the word's letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone ought to be capable of writing a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'compose' looks like writing music but tells you to rearrange LYRIC into a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name, so a male person.

clue.text: Muster in the bakery?

parts.note: a bakery holds bread buns, so reading the names aloud there would be a literal summons of buns

explanation.surface: Gathering the staff together at the baker's shop.
explanation.walkthrough: A roll is both a bread bun and a list of names, so a register taken at the baker's becomes a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling out names to see who is present is a muster, an assembly checked by list.

clue.text: This the colour of the blue boar, or red lion?

definitions.text: This the colour of the blue boar, or red lion?

parts.words: This the colour of the blue boar, or red lion?
parts.note: the Blue Boar and Red Lion are typical English pub names, and the phrase for regional atmosphere is this word plus colour

explanation.surface: A question about the colours of two heraldic beasts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Blue Boar and Red Lion are traditional names of English pubs; the neighbourhood pub is called one's local, and 'local colour' is regional flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: The neighbourhood pub is a regular's nearby drinking place.

clue.text: Matilda was not half peculiar!

indicators.note: not half means the first half of the word that follows is left out

explanation.surface: An indignant insistence that Matilda was very strange indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: Belloc's cautionary tale 'Matilda, who told Lies, and was Burned to Death' gives the definition; 'not half' (British slang for 'very') signals dropping the first half of PECULIAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilaire Belloc's verse heroine Matilda habitually told untruths.

clue.text: Vehicle, for the training of players?

definitions.meaning: a horse-drawn carriage that once ran scheduled routes
a theatre tutor who drills actors would be a coach for the boards

explanation.definitionFit: A horse-drawn passenger carriage, and jokingly a drama instructor for actors on the boards.

clue.text: What bowlers need not pay trick-cyclists for

definitions.text: What bowlers need not pay trick-cyclists for

parts.words: What bowlers need not pay trick-cyclists for
parts.note: a cricket bowler's figures are printed free in the scorebook, while psychiatrists, slangily trick-cyclists, charge for their sessions

explanation.surface: Advice that cricketers can skip paying circus performers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trick-cyclist' is British slang for a psychiatrist; a bowler's analysis is his wickets and runs conceded in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowler's figures and a psychiatrist's examination of the mind share this name.

clue.text: One of two navigational hazards

parts.note: in Greek myth sailors in the Strait of Messina had to pass between a rock monster and a whirlpool

explanation.surface: A note that sailors face a pair of perils.
explanation.walkthrough: Charybdis was the whirlpool; the other peril was a six-headed monster on a rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's Odyssey sets a sea monster beside the whirlpool Charybdis, a pair of perils for mariners.
